SUIT FOR RECOVERY OF Rs.43,29,026/
JUDGMENT 1.
Vide this Judgment, I intend to dispose off the suit for recovery of Rs. 43,29,026/ inclusive of interest against the defendants.
2. The factual matrix of the case is that the Plaintiff is the sole proprietor of M/s. Groovy Foods, a proprietorship concern and is engaged in the business of cocoa powder and industrial chocolates.

In pursuit of its business, it imported 'cocoa powder from the producer/seller "Altinmarka" in Turkey vide two consignments after payment in advance in the year 2013 in respect whereof NOC was also obtained from defendant no. 2 Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (in short "FSSAI")
prior to clearance from Customs as per procedure.

The plaintiff again imported "cocoa powder" from Shri Anil Grover vs The Secretary on 31 August, 2022 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/110959933/
1 Altinmarka after making the advance payment for the goods vide invoice no. 9199465 dated 31.12.2013 for an amount of Rs.12,15,879/ and paid freight charges of Rs.96,430/ to freight forwarder and the goods arrived in India on 24.01.2014.

sentences.text: The bill of entry no. 4478803 dated 28.01.2014 was filed which was okayed by Customs and duty amount of Rs.6,64,349/ was paid 30.01.2014.
As per requirement of the Customs, the plaintiff applied for NOC to FSSAI for these goods after paying sampling charges of Rs.6742/ on 07.02.2014.

However surprisingly they received an email from FSSAI on 08.02.2014 with remarks against  'Visual inspection details: Any Rectifiable Discrepancy Observed" "Yes" but no reason or alleged discrepancy was set out therein nor any details of sample withdrawn or result of sample analysis disclosed.

Vide letter dated 10.02.2014, the plaintiff was informed CS DJ No. 224/2017 page no. 2 of 16 that NOC cannot be accepted for the reason that the ingredient list was not mentioned on the label as per alleged mandatory labeling requirements under FSSAI regulations.

The plaintiff immediately submitted a detailed representation dated 11.02.2014 to Mr. S. Dave, Advisor of FSSAI giving details of earlier imports which were cleared with NOC from FSSAI and referring to the FSSAI regulations and Codex 105 standards and submitted copies of all previous bill of entries alongwith previous NOC issued by FSSAI for the same product.

He finally met Mr. Dave on 25.02.2014 and explained and clarified in detail that the product as imported carried the labeling as per FSSAI regulation and Codex 105 standard only and he was assured that he would receive a response within 48 hours.
However there was no response from FSSAI despite sending several emails to them.

Due to this enormous delay on the part of FSSAI and its failure to correctly apply its own regulations inspite of consistent follow up by the plaintiff led to heavy financial burden and the plaintiff was left with no option but to re export the shipment since he could not get the clearance.
The permission to reexport was granted on 24.10.2014 subject to fine and penalty of Rs.1,00,000/ and Rs.50,000/.

Apart from that the plaintiff firm also paid the detention charges of Rs.3,72,583/ and Rs.4,53,409/ on 29.10.2014 to Oriental Overseas Container Line plus storage charges of Rs.3,88,700/ to CONCOR and customs clearance charges of Rs.1,25,372/ on 30.10.2014 plus Rs.1,06,032/ paid to the freight forwarder for re export on 05.12.2014.
However the penalty amount was refunded by the defendant on 06.08.2015 in view of the order passed by the Commissioner of Appeals.

Thereafter plaintiff got issued legal notice dated 08.11.2016 to the defendant thereby demanding the said charges but defendants neither CS DJ No. 224/2017 page no. 3 of 16 replied the said notice nor made any payment which compelled the plaintiff to knock at the doors of the Court for payment of said amount through the present suit.

3. Summons sent to defendant no. 1 received back served on 14.02.2017 however none appeared on their behalf nor the written statement was filed within the stipulated period and hence their right to file the written statement was closed and they were proceeded exparte vide order dated 16.03.2017.

3.1 Defendant no. 2 filed detailed written statement taking preliminary objections to the effect that the plaintiff has not complied with the provisions of Food and Safety Act, 2006 and its rules and regulations; that vide letter dated 10.02.2014 it was clarified that product of the plaintiff cannot be assessed without knowing the ingredients which ought to have been mentioned as per the mandatory labeling requirements contained in FSS Regulations, 2011; that the product of the plaintiff was non conforming to section 23 of FSS Act and Regulations 2.2.2.2 and 2.6.1 of the FSS (Packaging and Labeling Regulations), 2011 and the plaintiff had deliberately not uploaded the copy Shri Anil Grover vs The Secretary on 31 August, 2022 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/110959933/
2 of the label in Food Import Clearance System (FICS); that the existing label of the product of the plaintiff is in violation of the said regulations.
3.2 In reply on merits, defendant no. 2 has denied all the material contents of the suit and prayed for its dismissal.
3.3 The plaintiff has filed replication to the written statement of defendant no. 2 thereby reaffirming and reiterating the contents of plaint and denying the contents of written statement.

4. From the pleadings of the parties, following issues were framed vide CS DJ No. 224/2017 page no.
4 of 16 order dated 07.07.2017:
1.
Whether plaintiff is entitled to the recovery of the suit amount in prayer clause (a) of the suit?
OPP 2. Whether plaintiff is entitled to interest, if yes, at what rate and for what period?
OPP 3.
Whether the plaintiff has complied with the provisions of Food and Safety Act, 2006 and its rules and regulations in terms of preliminary objections detailed in para1 of WS?
OPD 4. Relief.

Thereafter, matter was fixed for plaintiff's evidence.
5.
In order to prove its case, the plaintiff examined four more witnesses apart from him.
He examined himself as PW1 and reiterated the facts of plaint in his affidavit Ex.PW1/A.
He has relied upon the documents i.e. Ex. PW1/1 to Ex. PW1/44.

He was extensively crossexamined by ld.
Counsel for the defendant no. 2.

5.1 PW2 Shri Amarnath, Senior Manager, Dena Bank was summoned to prove payment made towards various charges by the plaintiff which are exhibited as Ex. PW2/1 (colly.) to Ex. PW2/6.
5.2 PW3
Shri Naveen Meena, Clerk, Bank of India was summoned to prove payment made towards Customs duty by the plaintiff which are exhibited as Ex.PW3/1 to Ex. PW3/3.
Shri Yash Jain, Service Delivery Manager, Indusind Bank was summoned to prove the statement of account and exhibited the same as Ex. PW4/1 (colly.) to Ex. PW4/3.

5.4 PW5 Shri Vikas Kumar, Deputy Manager, ICICI Bank was CS DJ No. 224/2017 page no. 5 of 16 Shri Anil Grover vs The Secretary on 31 August, 2022 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/110959933/
3 summoned to prove the transaction details which are exhibited as Ex.PW5/1 to Ex. PW5/6.

sentences.text: Thereafter, matter was fixed for defendant's evidence.
5.5 In defence, defendant no. 2 examined two witnesses.
They examined their Deputy Director Shri Anil Mehta as DW1.
He has tendered his evidence by way of affidavit Ex. DW1/A thereby reiterating the defence taken in the written statement.

He has relied on the documents i.e. Ex.
DW1/1 (colly.).
He was extensively cross examined by the counsel for the plaintiff.

5.6 DW2 Ms. Lydia Sona Lizzy, Technical Officer tendered her evidence by way of affidavit Ex.
DW2/A and she relied on documents already exhibited by DW1.
She was extensively cross examined by the counsel for the plaintiff.
Thereafter, matter was fixed for final arguments.
6. I have heard Ld. counsel for both the parties and meticulously gone through the record.
7. My issuewise findings are as follows: Issue nos. 1, 2 and 3 1.
Whether plaintiff is entitled to the recovery of the suit amount in prayer clause (a) of the suit?
OPP 2. Whether plaintiff is entitled to interest, if yes, at what rate and for what period?
OPP 3. Whether the plaintiff has complied with the provisions of Food and Safety Act, 2006 and its rules and regulations in terms of preliminary objections detailed in para1 of WS?
OPD 8.

All these issues are taken up together since they are interconnected involving the common point of discussion and finding on one issue will CS DJ No. 224/2017 page no. 6 of 16 have bearing on the other.
The onus to prove issue no. 1 and 2 was placed upon the plaintiff and that of issue no. 3 was upon the defendant.
9. The plaintiff has filed present suit for the recovery of Rs.43,29,026/.

He entered into the witness box as PW1 and has deposed that he is the sole proprietor of M/s. Groovy Foods, a proprietorship concern and is engaged in the business of cocoa powder and industrial chocolates; that he imported 'cocoa powder from the producer/seller "Altinmarka" in Turkey vide two consignments after payment in advance in the year 2013 in respect whereof NOC was also obtained from FSSAI prior to clearance from Customs as per procedure; that on each occasion the samples were withdrawn by FSSAI and NOC was issued after testing only; that he again imported "cocoa powder" from Altinmarka after making the advance payment for the goods vide invoice no. 9199465 dated 31.12.2013 for an amount of Rs.12,15,879/ and paid freight charges of Rs.96,430/ to freight forwarder and the goods arrived in India on 24.01.2014; that the bill of entry no. 4478803 dated 28.01.2014 was filed which was okayed by Customs and duty amount of Rs.6,64,349/ was paid 30.01.2014; that as per requirement of the Customs, the plaintiff applied for NOC to FSSAI for these goods after paying sampling charges of Rs.6,742/ on 07.02.2014 however surprisingly they received an email from FSSAI on 08.02.2014 with remarks against  'Visual inspection details: Any Rectifiable Discrepancy Observed" "Yes" but no reason or alleged discrepancy was set out therein Shri Anil Grover vs The Secretary on 31 August, 2022 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/110959933/
4 nor any details of sample withdrawn or result of sample analysis disclosed; that vide letter dated 10.02.2014, the plaintiff was informed that NOC cannot be accepted for the reason that the ingredient list was not mentioned on the label as per CS DJ No. 224/2017 page no. 7 of 16 alleged mandatory labelling requirements under FSSAI regulations.
From this point, the story of the defendant starts.

DW1 as well as DW2 have deposed that during the visual inspection, it was found that the labeling of the product of the plaintiff was in noncompliance of Regulation 2.2.2.2 of FSS (Packaging and Labeling) Regulations, 2011 and guidelines that were issued by FSSAI bearing no. 117/FSSAI/T/2010 (part J) dated 23.03.2012; that the list of ingredients is a mandatory requirement which needs to be fulfilled; that imported products are not a single ingredient products but are combination of two or more ingredients, therefore, they were in violation of aforementioned regulation 2.2.2.2 of FSS (Packaging and Labeling) Regulations, 2011 and guidelines that were issued by FSSAI bearing no. 117/FSSAI/T/2010 (part J) dated 23.03.2012; that regulation 2.2.2.2 of FSS (Packaging and Labeling) Regulations, 2011 is being reproduced herein below for ready reference:
"2.2.2 Labelling of prepackaged Foods  In addition to the General Labelling requirements specified in 2.2.1 above every package of food shall carry the following information on the label namely:
1. xxxx 2. List of Ingredients:

10. Per contra PW1 has deposed that "the plaintiff had with utmost caution and diligence gone through all the procedural requirements regarding labelling of his import which related to "wholesale packages"
and in respect whereof, sub section 4 of Article 2.6.1 provides as following:
Shri Anil Grover vs The Secretary on 31 August, 2022 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/110959933/
5 "In case of wholesale packages the particulars regarding list of ingredients, date of manufacture/packing, best before, expiry date, labelling of irradiated food and,
vegetarian logo/non vegetarian logo, may not be specified"
That the plaintiff had imported a wholesale package of Cocoa powder and hence the above mentioned particulars did not need to be mentioned.
The plaintiff had therefore complied with requirements"

11. The said stand of plaintiff is countered by the defendants vide para no. 4 of preliminary submissions wherein it is submitted that the guidelines that were issued by FSSAI bearing number 117/FSSAI/T/2010 dated 23.03.2012 clearly mentioned in para1:
CS DJ No. 224/2017 page no. 9 of 16 "

In respect of labeling requirements of different kinds of packages of foods consignments that are being imported in India, the requisite changes are required to be made in the Food Safety and Standards (Packagings and labeling) Regulations 2011.

entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: It has been decided by the Competent Authority that for smooth clearance of imported food items till the changes are incorporated in the FSS Regulations, 2011, different kinds of packages of food consignments that are being imported in India should carry the labeling information as enlisted below: S. No. Type of package Minimum Label Recruitments

1 . xxxxxxxxx xxxxxxx 2. Wholesale packages (including 1. Name of food semifurnished/intermediary food 2. List of ingredients (not products which will be further required in case of single processed to make final product and ingredient) packaged or prepacked food) 3. Name and complete address of the manufacturer 4. Date of manufacture
3. xxxxxxxx xxxxxx 12.
Starting from the beginning, Section 23 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 speaks about the packaging and labelling of goods.

It states that "no person shall manufacture, distribute,
sell or expose for sale of dispatch or deliver to any agent or broker for the purpose of sale, any packaged food products which are not market and labelled in the manner as may be specified by regulations:"

The regulation concerned is Section 2.2.2.2 of Food Safety and Standards (Packaging And Labelling) Regulation, 2011 which provides for exemption from filing list of CS DJ No.
224/2017 page no. 10 of 16 ingredients in case of wholesale packages.

entities.text: Food Safety and Standards (Packaging And Labelling) Regulation, 2011
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: It states that "In case of wholesale packages the particulars regarding list of ingredients.
Date of manufacture/ packing, best before, expiry date labelling of irradiated food and, vegetarian logo/ non vegetarian log, may not be specified."
and it is not in dispute that the plaintiff imported the goods for commercial/ industrial use by wholesale in India.
However, the defendant further relied on guidelines issued by FSSAI bearing no. 117/FSSAI/T/2012 dated 23.03.2012 which makes list of ingredients mandatory in all goods imported in India.

The end result is that the guideline is contradicting a regulation and the Shri Anil Grover vs The Secretary on 31 August, 2022 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/110959933/
6 question is that which of them will survive and it is the regulation indeed since it will comply the provisions of section 18(1), 91 and 92 of the Food Safety and Security Act.

sentences.text: The Hon'ble Bombay High Court in "Vital Nutraceuticals Pvt. Ltd. Vs. Union of India & Anr., dated 30.06.2014" has held that ".....The Food Authority which is obliged to do something by way of framing regulations, cannot be allowed to do the same by issuing advisories.

entities.text: Vital Nutraceuticals Pvt. Ltd. Vs. Union of India & Anr
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: This will not only cause prejudice to the FBOs but would also be contrary to the provisions of the FSS Act....".
The said judgment has been upheld by the Hon'ble Supreme Court vide judgment dated 19.08.2015 passed in "Food Safety and Standards Authority of India Vs. Vital Nutraceuticals Pvt. Ltd. & Ors."

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 13. Secondly, PW1 has deposed that it is even otherwise not even required on packages which are not wholesale also to declare all ingredients on the label when the other ingredients constitutes less than five percent (5%) of the food.

That the ingredients such as potassium carbonate and citric acid constitutes less than five percent (5%) of the food the catalogue/ingredient certificate of the product dated 10.02.2014 CS DJ No. 224/2017 page no. 11 of 16 submitted to defendant no. 2 sets out the percentage of the ingredients."

13.1 Section 2.2.2.2 (2) (d) of the Food Safety and Standards (Packaging And Labelling) Regulation, 2011, provides "where an ingredient itself is the product of two or more ingredient, such as compound ingredients shall be declared in the list of ingredients,
and shall be accompanied by a list, in brackets, of its ingredients in descending order of weight or volume, as the case may be;
Provided that where a compound ingredient, constitutes less than five percent of the food, the list of ingredient of the compound ingredient, other than food additive, need not to be declared;"
13.2

entities.text: Food Safety and Standards (Packaging And Labelling) Regulation, 2011
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: The stand of the plaintiff is that the imported good was not a single ingredient but combination of two or more ingredients and the other ingredient constitute less than 5 % of the food.
The Catalogue/Ingredient Certificate is Ex.P32.

DW1 has admitted that the imported good was not a single ingredient product but were combination of two or more ingredients and as per the said certificate the compound ingredient constitute less than 5 % of the food and in that situation there was no need of putting the list of ingredient on the label as per the said regulation.

14. Thirdly, admittedly, the email received from FSSAI on 08.02.2014 speaks about the remarks against  'Visual inspection details: Any Rectifiable Discrepancy Observed" "Yes" which means that the defect was the one which can be rectified.

The dictionary meaning of the word "rectify" as per Cambridge dictionary is to correct something or make something right meaning thereby the defect was not such which was going against the object of section 25 of the Food Safety and Standards Act,
2006.

The objective of section 25 of the Food Safety and Standards CS DJ No.
224/2017 page no. 12 of 16 Act, 2006 (hereinafter called the 'Act') is to ensure safety and wholesomeness of food being consumed by the diverse Indian populace as is evident from a perusal of the Preamble to the Act, which reads as follows: "An Act to consolidate the laws relating to food and to establish the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India for laying down science based standards for articles of food and to regulate their manufacture, storage, distribution, sale and import, to ensure Shri Anil Grover vs The Secretary on 31 August, 2022 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/110959933/
7 availability of safe and wholesome food for human consumption and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto."

sentences.text: 15. The fact that the goods in question were not breaching the safety parameters stood established by the statement made by defendants that "the samples were drawn but the same were not sent to the laboratory".

Furthermore, vide letter dated 11.02.2014 plaintiff expressed his desire to rectify the said defect but was never given the opportunity to do so despite repeated reminders through email due to which plaintiff was made to re export the goods thereby causing losses to him.
IN view of the same, plaintiff is entitled to recover the said losses.
16. Coming to the bifurcation of the amount claimed by the plaintiff.

The plaintiff has filed the present suit for the recovery of Rs.43,29,026/ regarding which PW1 has deposed that he paid amount of Rs.12,15,879/ and paid freight charges to freight forwarder; that the goods arrived in India on 24.01.2014 and the bill of entry 4478803 dated 28.01.2014 was filed which was okayed by customs and duty paid of amount of Rs.6,64,349/ on 30.01.2014.

The true copy of invoice no.
919465 dated 31.12.2013, packing list dated 31.12.2013, bill of lading dated 05.01.2014, CS DJ No.
224/2017 page no. 13 of 16 bank proof dated 26.12.2013 (advance payment), bill of entry no.
4478803 dated 28.01.2014 and duty payment proof dated 30.01.2014 and bill of freight forwarder/custom clearance are as Ex. P1 to P7.
The total value of the goods imported is shown as 14.25000 Euro as per Ex.PW1/1 which comes out to be Rs.12,12,960/ as per Ex. PW1/4.
The defendants have admitted the commercial invoice, packing list, bill of lading, bill of entry and duty payment proof and bill of freight.
Regarding the custom duty PW1 has deposed that plaintiff applied for duty draw back after reexport of above goods on 09.01.2015 and received duty drawback of Rs.6,34,208/ on 06.08.2015.

17. PW1 has further deposed that the permission for reexport was granted on 24.10.2014 to him subject to fine and penalty amounting to Rs.1,00,000/ and Rs.50,000/ but he has also deposed that he received penalty refund of Rs.50,000/ on 06.08.2015.

The copy of application for re export, permission allowed with fine and penalty, fine and penalty proof dated 03.07.2014 are Ex.
PW1/35 and PW1/36.
Though defendant no. 2 has not admitted the levy of said penalty but has not produced any contrary record to prove otherwise.

PW4, the witness from plaintiff's bank, has proved that plaintiff paid the said penalty and fine vide demand draft and hence he is entitled to recover the penalty amount of Rs.1,00,000/.
18.

PW1 has further deposed that he also paid the detention charges of Rs.3,72,583/ and Rs.4,53,409/ on 29.10.2014 to Oriental Overseas Container Line plus storage charges of Rs.3,88,700/ to CONCOR and customs clearance charges of Rs.1,25,372/ on 30.10.2014 plus Rs.1,06,032/ paid to the freight forwarder for reexport on 05.12.2014; that he also had to pay customs clearance charges of Rs.1,25,372/ on CS DJ No. 224/2017 page no. 14 of 16 30.10.2014.

Copy of detention charges paid to OOCL dated 14.07.2014 and 29.10.2014, CONCOR storage charges paid dated 30.10.2014 and bill of freight forwarder for reexport are marked Ex. P37 to P 39 and PW5 has proved that the plaintiff paid the said storage and detention charges.

The plaintiff has sought detention and storage charges till 29.10.2014 but it is not in dispute that the NOC was rejected by the defendant no. 2 vide email on 10.02.2014 and in that situation the said charges till Shri Anil Grover vs The Secretary on 31 August, 2022 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/110959933/
8 29.10.2014 cannot be justified.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
In view of the same, the plaintiff is entitled to recover the said charges from the date goods arrived in India till February, 2014 when the NOC was rejected which comes around ten percent of the total storage and detention charges of Rs.12,14,692/ and said ten percent is Rs.2,14,692/.
19.
Coming to the custom clearance charges, PW1 has relied on invoice dated 26.11.2014 for Rs.1,25,372/ but no payment receipt has been annexed with the said invoice.
However the fact that consignment was ultimately reexported and that cannot be done without the custom clearance.
In view of the same, plaintiff is entitled to recovery of said amount from the defendant no. 2.

In all plaintiff is entitled to recover value of the imported goods which is Rs.12,12,960/ plus penalty amount of Rs.1,00,000/ plus Rs.2,12,692/ towards storage and detention charges and custom clearance charges of Rs.1,25,372/ which comes to the total of Rs.16,51,024/ from the defendant no.2.
20.
Coming to the interest issue, the aforesaid findings confirms that defendant no. 2 withheld the dues of plaintiff without any just reason and excuse.

The plaintiff has claimed interest @ 18% per annum on the amount claimed but he has failed to bring any contractual stipulation to the effect CS DJ No. 224/2017 page no. 15 of 16 that he was entitled to any interest upon the said amount.

However, since he has been denied enjoyment of his outstanding sum, I am of the opinion that he deserves to be compensated for the said loss as the said sum could have been gainfully invested by him in some fruitful venture.
Consequently, plaintiff is awarded interest @ 9% per annum with effect from the date of filing of the present suit till the date of realization of decretal amount.
21. In view of the aforesaid discussion, issue no. 1 is partly decided in favour of plaintiff and partly against him and issue no. 2 is decided in favour of the plaintiff.
Issue no.3 is accordingly decided against the defendants.
Relief.
22. In view of findings on aforesaid issues, the suit of the plaintiff is hereby partly decreed and partly dismissed.

The suit is hereby decreed for an amount of Rs.16,51,024/ against defendant no. 2 along with pendente lite and future interest @ 9% per annum from the date of filing of the suit till the date of realization.
The cost of the suit is also awarded in favour of the plaintiff.
Decree sheet be prepared accordingly including the pleader fee.
File be consigned to Record Room.

"2.2.2 Labelling of prepackaged Foods  In addition to the General Labelling requirements specified in 2.2.1 above every package of food shall carry the following information on the label namely:
1. xxxx 2. List of Ingredients:
The Hon'ble Bombay High Court in "Vital Nutraceuticals Pvt. Ltd. Vs. Union of India & Anr., dated 30.06.2014" has held that ".....The Food Authority which is obliged to do something by way of framing regulations, cannot be allowed to do the same by issuing advisories.
13.1 Section 2.2.2.2 (2) (d) of the Food Safety and Standards (Packaging And Labelling) Regulation, 2011, provides "where an ingredient itself is the product of two or more ingredient, such as compound ingredients shall be declared in the list of ingredients,
and shall be accompanied by a list, in brackets, of its ingredients in descending order of weight or volume, as the case may be;
Provided that where a compound ingredient, constitutes less than five percent of the food, the list of ingredient of the compound ingredient, other than food additive, need not to be declared;"
